unsupervised-learning.name: Unsupervised Learning
unsupervised-learning.bio: Podcast: Ep 90: AI Pioneer Jürgen Schmidhuber on the State of AI Today

html_en:
OpenAI's GPT-5.6 launch dominated the AI conversation today, but the real story is subtler: a maturing industry grappling with UX complexity, competitive dynamics, and what "intelligence" actually costs at enterprise scale.

The GPT-5.6 Moment — and Its Messy Edges

OpenAI shipped GPT-5.6 "Sol" today alongside siblings Terra and Luna, and by most accounts the flagship model is a genuine step up. Sam Altman framed the launch around enterprise economics:

"We have heard enterprises on their concerns about AI costs, and 5.6 Sol is a huge step forward for dollars-per-task, as are Terra and Luna."
Box's Aaron Levie backed that up with real benchmark data, showing Sol outperforming GPT-5.5 across healthcare, financial services, public sector, and life sciences tasks — sometimes dramatically (healthcare jumped from 46% to 58%). His gloss: Sol "reasons from the source definitions and checks the documents rather than taking them at face value."

Thomas Sottiaux at OpenAI marked the launch by resetting usage limits twice across ChatGPT Work and Codex, explicitly inviting users to "try ambitious tasks." The generous rate-limit resets are a smart onboarding move for a product that requires sustained use to reveal its strengths.

But Peter Yang offered the most honest user-level review, mixing genuine admiration with pointed UX critique. His best compliment:

"It's got that dog in it. It basically never gives up, no matter how complicated a task you give it."
His concerns were equally direct — the Work vs. Codex split is confusing ("So developers aren't working?"), the Sol/Terra/Luna tiers lack explanatory UI, and the task vs. chat separation buries existing chat history. "The sooner this is all unified, the better," he wrote in his full breakdown.

Nikunj Kothari captured the week's whiplash in a comedic thread framed as an explanation to his wife:

"Fable 5 just came back online after the government suspended it for three weeks. The best coding model on earth was literally grounded. It's back now, and the rumored GPT-6 is being retrained specifically to beat it... And btw it's just Thursday."

The Competitive Map Is Redrawing Itself

The launch didn't happen in a vacuum. Guillermo Rauch flagged that model release week extends well beyond OpenAI:

"I suspect Meta Spark 1.1, Grok 4.5, and GLM 5.2 will significantly displace token market share. Most agentic tasks require reasonably high intelligence at fast speeds."
He also teased that "open models are about to get exorbitantly fast" — watch this space.

Amjad Masad of Replit put the broader dynamic bluntly:

"Just 6 months ago VCs suffered Anthropic psychosis and convinced themselves that it was going to be a monopoly. They will keep making great models, but so will the others, including new entrants."
The market, in other words, is working exactly as it should.

Levie zoomed out to the strategic question that will define the next decade: if every company in a vertical has access to the same frontier model, where does competitive advantage come from? His answer: the compounding loop between a company's proprietary data, its AI-connected workflows, and how employees interact with that system.

"There's no obvious point where this will become uniform across all companies in a vertical because each company will approach this in a different way, just as they already do with their talent and workflows."

AEO: The Invisible Marketing War

One of the day's more quietly provocative observations came from swyx, who noticed that AI models consistently recommend Resend for email infrastructure — even when users already have transactional email set up:

"Whoever does AEO for @resend needs to get a raise, all the leading frontier models keep trying to use Resend for emails even when I have existing transactional infrastructure already set up."
The tweet points to a nascent but increasingly important discipline: Answer Engine Optimization, or getting your product embedded in the training data and outputs of LLMs the way SEO once dominated Google. As AI becomes the default interface for technical decisions, being the model's default recommendation may matter as much as any other marketing channel.

Building on Solid Ground

As AI accelerates software development, Masad made a counterintuitive observation about what's happening to infrastructure:

"While AI is making coding less rigid, we're making the runtime more rigid. I'm noticing our infra teams writing formal specs for the first time. More deterministic systems. More resilient infrastructure. The faster you want to move, the more solid the ground beneath you has to be."
It's a useful corrective to the "vibe coding" narrative — the move-fast energy at the application layer depends on increasingly rigorous foundations underneath.

Meanwhile, Watch/Listen: Ep 90 of Unsupervised Learning features AI pioneer Jürgen Schmidhuber — credited by the New York Times as the "father of AI" — offering a bracingly long view. On how close we are to AGI:

"From a cosmic perspective, we are as close as we were in the 1970s... But is it going to be a couple of years or a couple of decades? I'm not totally sure about that because true AI is not just the AI behind the screen. True AI is also real robots, real machinery outside of the screen and in the physical world — and that's not working as well."
His skepticism on recursive self-improvement as a competitive moat, and his relative lack of concern about AI safety compared to peers, make for a useful counterweight to the week's launch-day excitement.

One More Thing

On a human note: Sam Altman expressed genuine sadness about an unnamed colleague's health situation — "this sucks" — a rare flash of unguarded emotion amid a week of product announcements. And @realmadhuguru announced joining Meta to build AI products, noting that while "SWE agents have transformed software engineering, agents in most other complex systems are still early. Most people haven't yet felt the full power of AI agents." It's the kind of talent signal worth tracking.
html_zh:
GPT-5.6 Sol的发布掀起了本周AI圈最大的波澜——但真正的故事，不只是一个新模型，而是整个行业正在重新洗牌。

🚀 Sol来了：OpenAI用GPT-5.6重新定义企业AI标准

本周最重磅的消息毫无悬念：OpenAI正式推出GPT-5.6，旗舰版本命名为Sol，另有Terra和Luna两个版本。@thsottiaux宣布，为庆祝发布，ChatGPT Work和Codex的使用额度将在24小时内重置两次，让用户尽情尝试高难度任务。

Sam Altman亲自下场，直接回应企业客户的痛点：

我们听到了企业对AI成本的顾虑，5.6 Sol在每任务成本上是巨大的进步，Terra和Luna亦然。

Box CEO Aaron Levie用真实数据佐证了Sol的实力。Box在企业文档集上的评测显示，Sol对比GPT-5.5的提升相当显著：金融服务（76% vs 71%）、医疗（58% vs 46%）、公共部门（74% vs 63%）。他总结道：

Sol从原始定义出发进行推理，而不是照单全收——它最可靠的地方，恰恰是数字驱动真实决策的地方。

产品经理出身的 @petergyang 给出了也许是本周最精准的评价："它骨子里有那股劲儿（It's got that dog in it）。"——不管任务多复杂，Sol从不轻言放弃。但他也指出，Sol、Terra、Luna的命名，加上Light/Medium/High不同档位，对普通用户来说实在太令人困惑了。

🌊 模型大爆发：竞争格局已彻底改变

如果说半年前VC圈还在幻想某家公司垄断模型市场，那这一周的现实已经给出了答案。Replit创始人 Amjad Masad 说得直白：

就在6个月前，VC们还患上了"Anthropic心理症"，说服自己那将是一家垄断企业。他们会继续出好模型，但其他人也会——包括新入场的玩家。

Vercel创始人 Guillermo Rauch 则列出了下一波冲击：Meta Spark 1.1、Grok 4.5、GLM 5.2即将显著争夺token市场份额。他补充道："开源模型的速度即将变得无比快。关注这个领域。"

Nikunj 用"向老婆解释这周模型发布"的段子，精准捕捉了这种信息爆炸的荒诞感——其中一句让人停顿：

美团开源了LongCat-2.0，1.6万亿参数，MIT协议。一家中国外卖公司，现在是前沿实验室了。你们的DoorDash等价物，现在在做前沿研究。

🛠️ 基础设施的反向逻辑：AI越快，底层要越稳

当AI让编码变得更随意、更流动，基础设施反而要走向更严格的对立面。Amjad Masad 观察到一个耐人寻味的现象：

我注意到我们的基础设施团队第一次开始写正式规范了。更确定性的系统，更具韧性的基础设施。你想跑得越快，脚下的地基就必须越扎实。

与此同时，@swyx 发现了一个有趣的AEO（AI引擎优化）现象：无论他已有什么邮件基础设施，主流前沿模型都会反复推荐用Resend发邮件。这可能是品牌在AI时代获得"心智占位"的最早案例之一。

🤖 Fable与Gemini：两个产品的不同姿态

本周还有两个值得关注的产品动态。Anthropic的Fable（此前因政府安全审查暂停三周）重新上线，多位建设者包括 @alexalbert__、@trq212 和 @amasad 都在第一时间转发演示，热情显而易见。

Gemini产品负责人 Josh Woodward 则展示了另一种产品文化——他在12小时内阅读了1400+条用户反馈，整理出十大需求，并逐一回应。Google Workspace集成稳定性排名第一，工具调用可靠性紧随其后。这种公开、具体的承诺，在大厂产品中并不多见。

🧠 深思：AI先驱Schmidhuber的冷眼旁观

在这片热闹之外，AI先驱Jürgen Schmidhuber在 Watch/Listen: Unsupervised Learning Ep 90 中给出了一盆冷水。他对AI技术乐观，但对模型公司的商业前景深感悲观，并认为当前的资本开支热潮严重过度。

真正的AI不只是屏幕背后的AI——它运作得很好，现在也能通过图灵测试了。但真正的AI还包括真实的机器人、真实的机械，在现实的物理世界里，那部分还远未实现。

他的结论耐人寻味：递归自我改进（RSI）不会成为任何一家公司的护城河。当所有人都在为本周的发布狂欢时，这个声音值得被记住。
